title: Why Your Card Wants You to Pay the Minimum
description: Why does your credit card company love the minimum payment? Penny follows one $85 payment to see where it really goes, and does the math on what 'just the minimum' costs.
sources: Federal Reserve Board, G.19 Consumer Credit release: commercial bank interest rate on credit card plans, accounts assessed interest (22.83% in August 2025, 22.30% in November 2025), federalreserve.gov/releases/g19

CFPB, Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.7(b)(12): every card statement must show the minimum payment warning, how long the balance takes to pay off at the minimum, and the total cost (Credit CARD Act of 2009)
CFPB, 'Consumer Credit Card Market Report' 2023: issuers typically set the minimum payment as a percentage of the balance plus interest and fees, with a dollar floor

Penny's calculation (shown on screen): $3,000 balance, 22% APR (monthly rate 22%/12), no new purchases; minimum = interest + 1% of the balance, at least $25 → 180 months (15 years), $4,433 interest, $7,433 paid in total. A flat $150 a month → 26 months, $771 interest.

lines.text: Why does your credit card want you to pay the minimum?
Say you owe three thousand dollars,
at twenty-two percent, about the average US card rate.
Your minimum payment is eighty-five dollars.
Easy, right? But watch where it goes.
Only thirty actually pays down your debt.
Keep paying just the minimum, and it takes fifteen years,
and about four thousand four hundred dollars in interest.
At a flat hundred and fifty every month,
it's gone in just over two years, with under eight hundred in interest.
So the minimum isn't a plan. It's their business model.
And your statement has to show you this math, by law.
